title: How a blockchain works
summary: See how fingerprints, links, and thousands of copies make a shared record almost impossible to rewrite.
objective: Explain why editing an old block breaks the chain and why the network rejects the edited copy.

hook.prompt: Bitcoin's full record of payments is public: anyone can download a copy. What stops someone from editing their copy to give themselves extra coins?

options.text: The record is encrypted, so nobody can change it
options.feedback: A common belief, but the record is readable by anyone. Its protection comes from somewhere else.

options.text: A company behind Bitcoin checks every change
options.feedback: There's no company or bank in charge. The checking is done another way.

options.text: The edit breaks the record's own links, and everyone else's copies disagree
Nothing: they can, but it's against the law
options.feedback: The design itself makes a forged copy useless, whatever the law says.

hook.explanation: The record checks itself, and thousands of other copies check it too. Let's see how.

bricks.title: Every block has a fingerprint
bricks.body: A blockchain is a record of transactions, like a shared notebook of payments. Transactions are grouped into batches called **blocks**. Each block gets a **hash**: a short code calculated from everything inside it. Change even one digit and the calculation gives a completely different hash. So a hash works like a fingerprint for the block's contents.

term.definition: A short code calculated from a block's contents. Any change to the contents gives a different hash.

bricks.prompt: Someone changes one payment in a block from 100 coins to 101. What happens to the block's hash?

options.text: It comes out completely different
It goes up by one, like the payment
options.feedback: A hash isn't a total of the amounts. It's a fingerprint: any change scrambles the whole code.

options.text: It stays the same, because the change is tiny
options.feedback: Size doesn't matter. Change even one digit and the hash comes out completely different.

bricks.hint: Think of the hash as a fingerprint of everything in the block.
bricks.explanation: The hash is recalculated from the block's contents, and any change, however small, gives a completely different code.

bricks.title: Each block holds the one before
bricks.body: So far, each block has a fingerprint. Now the chain: every block also stores the **previous block's hash**. Block 3 holds block 2's hash, and block 2 holds block 1's. Edit block 1 and its hash changes, so the copy stored in block 2 no longer matches. To hide the edit, you'd have to recalculate block 2, then block 3, and every block after.

term.definition: Blocks linked in order, each storing the hash of the block before it.

bricks.explanation: Block 3 still stores **2b9d**, but block 2's hash is now **e41c**. That mismatch is where the chain breaks.

bricks.prompt: A chain has 50 blocks. A cheater edits a payment in block 10. Which blocks must he recalculate to make his copy look unbroken again?

options.text: Only block 10
options.feedback: Block 11 stores block 10's old hash, so it breaks too, and so does every block after it.

options.text: Blocks 10 through 50
Blocks 1 through 10
options.feedback: Earlier blocks don't store later hashes. Each block only holds the hash of the one before it.

bricks.hint: Which blocks store a hash that depends on block 10?
bricks.explanation: Block 11 holds block 10's hash, block 12 holds block 11's, and so on, so every block from 10 to 50 must be redone.

bricks.title: Thousands of copies check each other
bricks.body: So far, an edit breaks the links, but a cheater could recalculate them. Here's what stops him. Thousands of computers, called **nodes**, each keep a full copy and check every new block against the rules. In Bitcoin, adding a block also takes **proof of work**: a huge amount of computing. Nodes keep the chain with the most work behind it, so a rewritten copy loses unless the cheater outpaces everyone.

term.definition: A computer that keeps its own full copy of the blockchain and checks new blocks.

visual.alt: Five computers linked in a network, each holding the same three-block chain.

bricks.prompt: A new block arrives that spends coins its sender never had. The proof of work on it is correct. What do the nodes do?

options.text: Each node rejects it, because it breaks the rules
They accept it, because the work was done
options.feedback: Work only makes a block costly to add. Each node still checks it against the rules, and spending coins you don't have breaks them.

options.text: They ask a central server whether to accept it
options.feedback: There's no central server. Every node does the checking itself.

bricks.hint: What does every node do with each new block?
bricks.explanation: Every node checks each new block against the rules on its own. A block that breaks them is rejected, however much work went into it.

bricks.prompt: A cheater wants to change one old payment. Which payment would be hardest to rewrite?

options.text: One in the newest block, added ten minutes ago
options.feedback: Only this one block needs redoing, so it's the easiest target. Each newer block adds more work to redo.

options.text: One from a year ago, with thousands of blocks after it
Both are equally hard: one edit is one edit
options.feedback: The edit breaks every later link, so the number of blocks after it decides how much work must be redone.

bricks.hint: Count how many blocks would need their work redone.
bricks.explanation: Every block after the edit must be redone with fresh proof of work, faster than the whole network. Thousands of blocks make that practically impossible.

challenge.prompt: Mia edits a week-old payment in her copy, then types the block's old hash back in so the next block still matches. She shares her copy. What happens?

options.text: Nodes recalculate the hash from the edited contents, see it doesn't match, and keep their own chain
It works: the links match again, so nodes accept her copy
options.feedback: A hash isn't something you type in. Nodes calculate it from the block's contents, and the edited contents give a different hash.

options.text: It works on her copy, and the edit spreads to every node
options.feedback: Each node checks blocks itself and keeps the chain with the most work behind it, not whatever copy it's sent.

options.text: Bitcoin's company reverses her edit
options.feedback: No company runs it. Nodes reject the copy on their own by checking hashes and rules.

challenge.hint: Where does a block's hash come from?
challenge.explanation: A hash is calculated from contents, so a pasted-in old hash doesn't fit the edited block. Every node spots that and keeps the real chain.

takeaways: A block's hash is a fingerprint of its contents: change anything and the hash changes.
Each block stores the previous block's hash, so editing one block breaks every link after it.
Thousands of nodes keep copies and check every block, and proof of work makes rewriting old blocks too costly.
